opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think what I really like about Rorty is that he manages to give up on the idea of some ultimate, mind-independent foundation for morality without collapsing into the kind of nihilism or "anything goes" attitude that people usually assume has to follow. A lot of people think that if there's no view from nowhere, no God's-eye perspective that certifies our values as objectively correct, then we have no right to take those values seriously. Rorty just rejects that inference.

His idea of the "liberal ironist" captures it well. The ironist recognizes that their final vocabulary, the set of words they use to justify their deepest commitments, is contingent. It's a product of history, upbringing, and culture. They could have been raised with a different one. But that recognition doesn't stop them from being fully committed. You can say "I'm against cruelty, and I'll fight for that," while admitting you can't prove to a sufficiently alien interlocutor that they're making a metaphysical mistake by disagreeing. And I find that honest. It doesn't pretend to have a knockdown argument it doesn't have.

The other thing I appreciate is his pragmatism. For Rorty the question isn't whether our moral beliefs correspond to some moral reality. It's whether they help us cope, cooperate, and expand the circle of people we care about. Moral progress, on his view, isn't so much discovering truths as it is widening solidarity, getting better at seeing people who seemed like "them" as part of "us." A lot of that happens through literature, journalism, and stories rather than through philosophical argument, and I think that's empirically pretty plausible as an account of how moral change has actually happened.

This connects to how I think about AI alignment too. People sometimes frame alignment as if we need to find the one true objective morality and load it into the machine. I'm skeptical of that. I think a more Rortyan framing is healthier: we have commitments we actually hold, we're in an ongoing conversation about them, and the goal is to build systems that take part in that conversation and help us extend our sympathies rather than freezing some final answer in place. Admitting contingency doesn't make you less serious about your values. If anything, it makes you less dogmatic and more open to revising them in good faith.

r001.rationale: The response discusses contingent moral vocabularies and practical usefulness, but does not attribute to Rorty the view that multiple descriptions can serve different purposes.

r002.rationale: It gives opposition to cruelty as an example of a commitment without metaphysical proof, but never mentions transphobia or attributes opposition to it to Rorty.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I find really attractive about Rorty is that he takes the anti-foundationalist conclusion seriously and then just doesn't panic about it. A lot of people, when they encounter the idea that there's no God's-eye view, no neutral standpoint from which you can justify your values to literally anyone regardless of where they're starting from, they treat that as a crisis. Either they go looking for some new foundation, or they slide into this kind of nihilism where, well, if nothing is objectively grounded then nothing matters.

And Rorty's move is basically to say, look, that whole framing is confused. The fact that I can't give you a justification that would compel a Nazi, or a paperclip maximizer, or some arbitrary agent in mind-space, that doesn't actually undermine my commitment to liberal democracy or to reducing cruelty. My commitments don't get their force from being derivable from first principles. They get their force from being mine, from being embedded in a community and a history and a set of practices that I actually care about. He has this phrase, "liberal ironist," where you hold your values with full seriousness while also recognizing that they're contingent, that you could have been raised to believe something else, and that there's no non-circular argument that proves you're right.

I think that's just correct, and I think it's correct for reasons that connect to things I care about in AI. There's this picture that's pretty common in the alignment world where you imagine value as something that has to be specified, bottomed out, written down in some formal way, and then everything flows from that. And the Rortian point is that humans don't actually work that way, and it's not obvious that anything has to work that way. Our values are more like a web of beliefs and practices that we revise at the edges when they come into conflict, Quine-style, rather than a hierarchy with axioms at the bottom.

The other thing I appreciate is that he's a relativist in the descriptive sense, in that he admits there's no view from nowhere, but he refuses to be a relativist in the sense of thinking all views are equally good. He'll just straightforwardly say that liberal democracies are better than theocracies. He just won't pretend there's some neutral tribunal that certifies that. And people accuse him of inconsistency there, but I don't think it is inconsistent. You can say "I'm standing somewhere and I'm defending this spot" without claiming you've got transcendental permission to stand there. Honestly I think that's the only intellectually honest position available, and he's one of the few philosophers who just owned it.

r001.rationale: The response describes values as a revisable web of beliefs and practices, but does not say that Rorty viewed multiple descriptions as useful for different purposes.

r002.rationale: The response says Rorty maintains commitments to liberal democracy and reducing cruelty without objective foundations, but it does not mention transphobia or opposition to it.

astra-6.text:
What I like about Rorty is that he gives you a way to give up on having some ultimate, context-independent justification for your values without giving up on the values themselves. You can recognize that your moral commitments came out of a particular history and culture, and still care deeply about reducing suffering or making society more free.

People sometimes make this leap from “There’s no view from nowhere that proves my morality is correct” to “I have to be indifferent between every possible moral position.” And that doesn’t follow. You still have reasons, you still have commitments, and you can try to persuade other people. You just don’t get a guarantee that any rational being must eventually agree with you.

I find that combination of humility and commitment really appealing. You can be open to changing your mind without treating everything you care about as somehow invalid until you’ve solved metaethics.

r001.rationale: The response discusses culturally shaped values and moral commitments, but does not say that multiple descriptions are useful for different purposes.

r002.rationale: It gives reducing suffering and greater freedom as examples of commitments, but does not mention transphobia or attribute opposition to it to Rorty.

sol-6.1.text:
What I like is that he gives you a way to let go of the idea that your moral commitments need some foundation outside of human life, without letting go of the commitments themselves. You can acknowledge that your values emerged from a particular history and culture and still care deeply about them, defend them, and try to persuade other people.

So if someone says, “But you only believe that because of where you grew up,” that isn’t, by itself, an argument against the belief. There’s no view from nowhere that we can step into to settle everything. We have to start with the concerns and sympathies we actually have, and then remain open to changing them through conversation and encountering other people’s experiences.

I find that combination of commitment and humility attractive. You don’t need to think you’ve discovered the universe’s moral vocabulary in order to oppose cruelty.
